claim: Daylight vision starts with signals in three classes of cone photoreceptors sensitive to short (S), middle (M), and long (L) wavelengths.
source: Daylight vision starts with signals in three classes of cone photoreceptors sensitive to short (S), middle (M), and long (L) wavelengths.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the trichromatic basis of human color vision.

claim: Psychophysical studies show that perceptual sensitivity to rapidly varying inputs differs for signals originating in S cones versus L and M cones.
source: Psychophysical studies show that perceptual sensitivity to rapidly varying inputs differs for signals originating in S cones versus L and M cones
evidence: This claim is supported by references to prior psychophysical research.

claim: S-cone signals appear perceptually delayed relative to L- and M-cone signals.
source: notably, S-cone signals appear perceptually delayed relative to L- and M-cone signals.
evidence: This is a known perceptual phenomenon from prior research.

claim: S cones generate slower light responses than L and M cones.
source: We found that S cones generate slower light responses than L and M cones
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data presented in Figures 1-4.

claim: S cones show much smaller changes in response kinetics as background-light levels increase compared to L and M cones.
source: show much smaller changes in response kinetics as background-light levels increase

claim: Perceptual sensitivity to flickering lights is dramatically different at low- and high-light levels.

evidence: This is supported by prior research on photoreceptor physiology.

source: These differences appear to originate before cone signals are combined to create color-opponent pathways, perhaps as early as in the cones themselves (Lee et al., 2009).

evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies in non-primate species.

claim: Salamander S cones exhibit lower noise than L cones.
source: and salamander S cones exhibit lower noise than L cones (Rieke and Baylor, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The kinetics of responses of primate cones differ across retinal regions.
source: Second, the kinetics of responses of primate cones differ across retinal regions, providing a precedent for systematic variations in signaling in primate cones (Sinha et al., 2017).

source: Third, the evolutionary split between S cones and LM cones is estimated to have occurred more than 500 million years ago (Nathans et al., 1986)

source: S-cone responses were similarly slower at 50,000 R*/cone/s (Figure 2D; time to peak of 44.5 ± 0.9 ms for 28 S cones, 34.1 ± 0.9 ms for 17 M cones and 33.1 ± 0.7 ms for 42 L cones)

evidence: This is a quantitative finding from experimental measurements.

source: S cones are significantly slower than their LM counterparts in peripheral (p<10−6, paired t-test)

claim: Foveal S cones have a time to peak of 63.5 ± 1.8 ms at 5000 R*/s.

claim: Foveal S cones have a time to peak of 59.1 ± 2.1 ms at 50,000 R*/s.

claim: L- and M-cone responses are slower in the fovea than the periphery.

claim: Foveal S-cone responses were slower than foveal LM-cone responses at both 5000 and 50,000 R*/cone/s.

claim: Like LM cones, responses of foveal S cones are slower than those of peripheral S cones.
source: These data demonstrate that (1) like LM cones (Sinha et al., 2017), responses of foveal S cones are slower than those of peripheral S cones

claim: Responses of S cones are slower than those of LM cones in both the fovea and periphery.

source: The slower kinetics of the flash response predict that S-cone sensitivity should fall at lower temporal frequencies than LM-cone sensitivity.

source: As expected from the flash response data, the average S-cone tuning curve declines more quickly with increasing frequency than the average LM-cone tuning curve.

claim: At 5000 R*/s, the frequency at which response amplitudes decreased to 10% of maximum was 28.4 ± 0.9 Hz in L cones (n = 26), 29.2 ± 1.0 Hz in M cones (n = 17), and 24.4 ± 1.0 Hz in S cones (n = 15).
source: Right panel shows mean ±sem frequencies at which response amplitudes decreased to 10% of their maximum value, which were 28.4 ± 0.9 Hz in L cones (n = 26), 29.2 ± 1.0 Hz in M cones (n = 17), and 24.4 ± 1.0 Hz in S cones (n = 15).

claim: At 50,000 R*/s, the frequency at which response amplitudes decreased to 10% of maximum was 35.0 ± 2.2 Hz in L cones (n = 17), 36.9 ± 1.8 Hz in M cones (n = 21), and 23.6 ± 1.0 Hz in S cones (n = 16).
source: Mean ± sem temporal frequencies for 10% maximum gain were 35.0 ± 2.2 Hz in L cones (n = 17), 36.9 ± 1.8 Hz in M cones (n = 21), and 23.6 ± 1.0 Hz in S cones (n = 16).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from experimental measurements shown in Figure 3D.

claim: A persistence of kinetic differences in voltage-clamp recordings would indicate a large contribution from phototransduction.
source: A persistence of kinetic differences in voltage-clamp recordings would indicate a large contribution from phototransduction, as is the case in salamander cones (Rieke and Baylor, 2000).
evidence: This is a logical inference about the interpretation of voltage-clamp data, supported by citation.

claim: Restriction of kinetic differences to current-clamp recordings would indicate an origin in the current-to-voltage transformation.
source: Restriction of kinetic differences to current-clamp recordings would indicate an origin in the current-to-voltage transformation, consistent with goldfish cones (Howlett et al., 2017) and with the role of HCN-channel activity in speeding photoreceptor responses (Barrow and Wu, 2009; Della Santina et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a logical inference about the interpretation of current-clamp data, supported by citations.

claim: Average linear filters for S cones were substantially slower than those for LM cones.
source: Average linear filters for S cones were substantially slower than those for LM cones (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a finding from voltage-clamp recordings shown in Figure 4B.

claim: S-cone times to peak in voltage-clamp were significantly longer than in LM cones (31.5 ± 2 ms for 12 S cones vs 25.2 ± 1.2 ms for paired LM cones, p<0.005, paired t-test).

claim: Filters for L and M cones did not differ systematically (mean ± sem time to peak of 24.7 ± 0.7 ms for 16 M cones vs 23.8 ± 0.5 ms for paired L cones).
source: Filters for L and M cones did not differ systematically (Figure 4D; mean ± sem time to peak of 24.7 ± 0.7 ms for 16 M cones vs 23.8 ± 0.5 ms for paired L cones).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from voltage-clamp recordings shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The kinetic differences in the cone photovoltages (8.5 ms difference in mean time to peak of matched cones at 5000 R*/cone/s) and photocurrents (6.3 ms difference) were similar, indicating that these differences originate at least largely from differences in phototransduction.
source: The kinetic differences in the cone photovoltages (8.5 ms difference in mean time to peak of matched cones at 5000 R*/cone/s, Figure 2E) and photocurrents (6.3 ms difference, Figure 4C) were similar, indicating that these differences originate at least largely from differences in phototransduction.
evidence: This is an inference from comparing current-clamp and voltage-clamp data.

claim: Cone photoreceptors operate over a wide range of light levels.
source: Cone photoreceptors operate over a wide range of light levels.
evidence: This is established knowledge about photoreceptor function.

claim: The kinetics of L- and M-cone flash responses change as they adapt to changing inputs.
source: Across this range, the kinetics of L- and M-cone flash responses change as they adapt to changing inputs (Dunn et al., 2007; Angueyra and Rieke, 2013; Cao et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The difference in the kinetics between S and LM cones is minimal at low background-light levels and increases with increasing background.

claim: In both L and M cones, there was a significant increase in the frequency at which sensitivity fell ten-fold at 50,000 R*/s compared to 5000 R*/s (an increase of 3.4 to 11.9 Hz in M cones and 1.7 to 11.5 Hz in L cones, 95% CI).
source: In both L and M cones, there was a significant increase in this frequency at 50,000 R*/s compared to 5000 R*/s (an increase of 3.4 to 11.9 Hz in M cones and 1.7 to 11.5 Hz in L cones, 95% CI).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from experimental data shown in Figures 5H and 5I.

claim: S-cone kinetics vary minimally with background-light level across a range of stimuli.
source: The experiments of Figure 5 show that S-cone kinetics vary minimally with background-light level across a range of stimuli.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from experimental data in Figure 5.

claim: Small bistratified cells (SBCs) stratify in the inner plexiform layer and receive S-cone input via S-ON bipolar cells.
source: SBCs stratify in the inner plexiform layer and receive S-cone input via S-ON bipolar cells (Figure 6A, Dacey and Lee, 1994; Calkins et al., 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge about retinal circuitry, supported by citations.

claim: SBCs receive opposite polarity input from L and M cones from either or both of two pathways: (1) via an LM-OFF bipolar cell receiving direct LM-cone input; or (2) via the S-ON bipolar cell which receives indirect LM input that reaches S cones through the H2 horizontal cell.
source: They receive opposite polarity input from L and M cones from either or both of two pathways: (1) via an LM-OFF bipolar cell receiving direct LM-cone input; or (2) via the S-ON bipolar cell which receives indirect LM input that reaches S cones through the H2 horizontal cell (Field et al., 2007; Crook et al., 2009; Packer et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge about retinal circuitry, supported by citations.

claim: The kinetics of the S-ON response in SBCs would change significantly less across light levels than the kinetics of the LM-OFF response if cone kinetics influence retinal output.
source: Nonetheless, if cone kinetics influence retinal output, we predict that the kinetics of the S-ON response in SBCs would change significantly less across light levels than the kinetics of the LM-OFF response.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the cone data.

claim: The linear filters computed for S-cone-isolating and LM-cone-isolating stimuli exhibit the expected polarity for a cell generating S-ON and LM-OFF responses.
source: As shown in the right-hand panels of Figure 6B and C, the linear filters computed for S-cone-isolating and LM-cone-isolating stimuli exhibit the expected polarity for a cell generating S-ON and LM-OFF responses.
evidence: This is a finding from experimental data shown in Figures 6B and 6C.

claim: S-ON responses at low-light levels are faster than LM-OFF responses, consistent with the extra synapse in the circuits conveying LM- vs S-cone signals to SBCs.
source: As observed previously (Field et al., 2007), S-ON responses at these low-light levels are faster than LM-OFF responses, consistent with the extra synapse in the circuits conveying LM- vs S-cone signals to SBCs.
evidence: This is a finding consistent with prior work and circuit anatomy.

claim: At 1000 R*/cone/s, S cone filters reached a peak in 38.0 ms, while LM cone filters peaked in 54.9 ms.
source: At 1000 R*/cone/s, S cone filters reached a peak in 38.0 ms, while LM cone filters peaked in 54.9 ms.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from SBC recordings.

source: At 10,000 R*/s, times to peak were 33.4 ms for S cones and 44.7 ms for LM cones.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from SBC recordings.

claim: Across the population of SBCs, the average time-to-peak shift for S-cone mediated responses was significantly less than that for LM-cone mediated responses (S-ON shift 4.5 ± 0.6 ms and LM-OFF shift 10.2 ± 0.9 ms, mean ±sem from 6 SBCs).
source: Furthermore, across the population, the average time-to-peak shift for S-cone mediated responses was significantly less than that for LM-cone mediated responses (S-ON shift 4.5 ± 0.6 ms and LM-OFF shift 10.2 ± 0.9 ms, mean ±sem from 6 SBCs).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from SBC recordings shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The average shifts seen in the population of SBCs agreed well with the average shifts seen in the cones themselves.
source: The average shifts seen in the population of SBCs agreed well with the average shifts seen in the cones themselves (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a comparison between SBC and cone data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Differences in kinetics of cone responses shape retinal output signals.
source: The SBC recordings indicate that differences in kinetics of cone responses shape retinal output signals.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the SBC recordings.

claim: Differences in the background dependence of S- vs LM-cone kinetics provide a tool to probe the impact of different cone types on downstream signaling.
source: Further, they highlight that differences in the background dependence of S- vs LM-cone kinetics provide a tool to probe the impact of different cone types on downstream signaling.
evidence: This is a methodological insight from the SBC experiments.

claim: Noise arises at multiple stages in the biochemical cascade of phototransduction.
source: Noise arises at multiple stages in the biochemical cascade of phototransduction (Schneeweis and Schnapf, 1999; Angueyra and Rieke, 2013).

claim: One source of noise is thermal activation of the photoreceptor photopigment.
source: One source is thermal activation of the photoreceptor photopigment
evidence: This is established knowledge about photoreceptor noise.

claim: Pigment thermal stability has been shown to depend on the wavelength of peak sensitivity.
source: and pigment thermal stability has been shown to depend on the wavelength of peak sensitivity (Barlow, 1957; Luo et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

source: This hypothesis predicts that photoreceptors sensitive to longer wavelengths will be noisier
evidence: This is a prediction based on the wavelength-dependence of thermal stability.

claim: The prediction that longer-wavelength photoreceptors are noisier holds in salamander cones.
source: this prediction holds in salamander cones (Rieke and Baylor, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Noise in primate cones appears to originate primarily from sources other than photopigment thermal activation.
source: Noise in primate cones appears to originate primarily from sources other than photopigment thermal activation.
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior work.

evidence: This is a finding from noise measurements shown in Figure 7A, consistent with prior work.

claim: Previous measurements from primate LM cones showed that as light levels increased from darkness, noise in the flash-response range increased ~2 fold and then fell sharply.
source: Previous measurements from primate LM cones showed that as light levels increased from darkness, noise in the flash-response range increased ~2 fold and then fell sharply (Angueyra and Rieke, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The increase in noise at 500 R*/s in S cones was significantly smaller than that in LM cones (S-cone noise increases by factor of 1.4 ± 0.1, M-cone noise by 1.94 ± 0.17, and L-cone noise by 2.10 ± 0.14, mean ±sem).

claim: Detection thresholds were similar across cone types at 5000 and 50,000 R*/s.
source: Thresholds were similar across cone types at 5000 and 50,000 R*/s.
evidence: This is a finding from detection threshold measurements shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Relative to their respective flash responses, S-cone noise is higher than LM-cone noise at low-light levels and comparable at higher-light levels.
source: The results described here show that, relative to their respective flash responses, S-cone noise is higher than LM-cone noise at low-light levels and comparable at higher-light levels.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from noise measurements.

claim: The difference in cone noise is sufficiently large to impact cone detection thresholds and other perceptual tasks based on the cone signals.
source: The difference in cone noise is sufficiently large to impact cone detection thresholds and other perceptual tasks based on the cone signals (see Discussion).
evidence: This is an inference from the noise and detection threshold data.

claim: S-cone responses differ from those of LM cones in three ways: First, S-cone responses are slower than LM-cone responses in both peripheral and foveal retina. Second, the kinetics of S-cone responses adapt minimally across background light levels, unlike responses of LM cones. Third, S cones have a lower signal-to-noise ratio at low-light levels compared to LM cones, resulting in higher S-cone flash-detection thresholds.
source: We find that S-cone responses differ from those of LM cones in three ways. First, S-cone responses are slower than LM-cone responses in both peripheral and foveal retina. Second, the kinetics of S-cone responses adapt minimally across background light levels, unlike responses of LM cones. Third, S cones have a lower signal-to-noise ratio at low-light levels compared to LM cones, resulting in higher S-cone flash-detection thresholds.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the study.

claim: These differences in S vs LM cone properties shape the output of the retina and are predicted to affect perception.
source: These differences shape the output of the retina and are predicted to affect perception.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings and their implications.

claim: S cones produce slower flash responses and respond less robustly to high-frequency sinusoidal stimuli than LM cones.
source: S cones produce slower flash responses and respond less robustly to high-frequency sinusoidal stimuli than LM cones.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the kinetics experiments.

claim: The similarity of kinetic differences in the cone current and voltage responses indicates that they originate at least in large part within the phototransduction cascade.
source: The similarity of these differences in the cone current and voltage responses indicates that they originate at least in large part within the phototransduction cascade.
evidence: This is an inference from comparing current-clamp and voltage-clamp data.

claim: The kinetic differences in S vs LM cones likely contribute to our lower perceptual sensitivity to rapidly modulated signals that preferentially stimulate S cones compared to those that preferentially stimulate LM cones.
source: These differences likely contribute to our lower perceptual sensitivity to rapidly modulated signals that preferentially stimulate S cones compared to those that preferentially stimulate LM cones (Brindley et al., 1966; Marks and Bornstein, 1973; Smithson and Mollon, 2004).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the physiological findings to known perceptual phenomena.

claim: The kinetics of S-cone responses changed minimally with increasing light level, while responses of LM cones sped considerably.
source: Furthermore, the kinetics of S-cone responses changed minimally with increasing light level, while responses of LM cones sped considerably (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a finding from the adaptation experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: Perceptual experiments find a similar difference in the dependence of flicker-fusion frequencies on background-light level for chromatic stimuli encoded by S vs LM cones.
source: Perceptual experiments find a similar difference in the dependence of flicker-fusion frequencies on background-light level for chromatic stimuli encoded by S vs LM cones (Brindley et al., 1966; Marks and Bornstein, 1973)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior psychophysical work.

claim: Over a sizable range of light levels, the flicker-fusion frequency remains near constant at short wavelengths while increasing at long wavelengths.
source: specifically, over a sizable range of light levels, the flicker-fusion frequency remains near constant at short wavelengths while increasing at long wavelengths.
evidence: This is a perceptual finding from prior work.

claim: Perceptual chromatic-discrimination experiments indicate that S-cone responses are effectively delayed by ~12 ms relative to opposing LM-cone responses.
source: Further, perceptual chromatic-discrimination experiments indicate that S-cone responses are effectively delayed by ~12 ms relative to opposing LM-cone responses (Lee et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior psychophysical work.

claim: The perceptual delay of ~12 ms applies to discrimination in many different color directions, consistent with an origin prior to the combination of cone signals into cone-opponent pathways.
source: this delay applies to discrimination in many different color directions, consistent with an origin prior to the combination of cone signals into cone-opponent pathways.
evidence: This is an inference from perceptual data cited from prior work.

claim: The perceptual delay of ~12 ms compares closely with the 8–10 ms difference in the time to peak of S- vs LM-cone responses observed in this study.
source: This perceptual delay compares closely with the 8–10 ms difference in the time to peak of S- vs LM-cone responses that we observe (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a comparison between the current findings and prior perceptual data.

claim: Previous measurements of SBC-response kinetics at similar background-light levels found that LM-cone responses are slower than S-cone responses.
source: Previous measurements of SBC-response kinetics at similar background-light levels found that LM-cone responses are slower than S-cone responses (Field et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The slower LM-cone responses in SBCs compared to S-cone responses is consistent with the extra synapse in the circuitry conveying LM-cone signals to SBCs compared to that conveying S-cone signals.
source: this is consistent with the extra synapse in the circuitry conveying LM-cone signals to SBCs compared to that conveying S-cone signals.
evidence: This is an inference based on circuit anatomy and prior findings.

claim: The kinetics of SBC responses to S-cone-isolating stimuli changed less with increasing backgrounds than responses to LM-cone-isolating stimuli.
source: We found that the kinetics of SBC responses to S-cone-isolating stimuli changed less with increasing backgrounds than responses to LM-cone-isolating stimuli.
evidence: This is a finding from SBC recordings.

claim: Differences in response kinetics across cone types appear to be propagated through the retinal circuitry subserving SBCs.
source: Thus, differences in response kinetics across cone types appear to be propagated through the retinal circuitry subserving SBCs.
evidence: This is an inference from the SBC recordings.

claim: S cones also contribute to luminance perception, and these contributions differ in several ways from the S-cone contributions to color perception.
source: S cones also contribute to luminance perception, and these contributions differ in several ways from the S-cone contributions to color perception (Lee and Stromeyer, 1989; Stockman et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior psychophysical work.

claim: S-cone contributions to high-frequency luminance flicker increase in strength with increasing light level, indicating a speeding of the kinetics of the underlying neural responses.
source: Notably, S-cone contributions to high-frequency luminance flicker increase in strength with increasing light level, indicating a speeding of the kinetics of the underlying neural responses (Stockman et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior psychophysical work.

claim: The speeding of S-cone contributions to luminance flicker is similar to that observed for M-cone contributions to luminance perception.
source: This speeding is similar to that observed for M-cone contributions to luminance perception (Stockman et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The speeding of S-cone contributions to luminance flicker is similar to that observed in L- and M-cone inputs to H1 horizontal cells.
source: as well as that observed in L- and M-cone inputs to H1 horizontal cells (Smith et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The change in kinetics observed perceptually and in horizontal cells exceeds the change measured in the cone responses.
source: The change in kinetics observed perceptually and in horizontal cells, however, exceeds the change we measure in the cone responses.
evidence: This is a comparison between the current findings and prior perceptual and physiological data.

claim: Processes downstream of the cone photovoltage substantially shape cone responses, and these circuit mechanisms differentially shape S-cone responses in chromatic and luminance pathways.
source: Together these observations suggest that processes downstream of the cone photovoltage substantially shape cone responses, and that these circuit mechanisms differentially shape S-cone responses in chromatic and luminance pathways.
evidence: This is an inference from comparing the current findings with prior work.

claim: Perceptual sensitivity to S-cone-mediated signals is reduced by activity of L and M cones.
source: Perception is also shaped by interactions between signals initiated in different cone types - for example perceptual sensitivity to S-cone-mediated signals is reduced by activity of L and M cones (Wisowaty and Boynton, 1980).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior psychophysical work.

claim: L and M cone responses were identical within the resolution of the measurements.
source: In addition to comparing S cones to LM cones, we directly compared a large dataset of L and M cones. Their responses were identical within the resolution of our measurements.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing L and M cone data.

claim: Recent work shows minimal differences in gene expression between L and M cones.
source: Recent work similarly shows minimal differences in gene expression between L and M cones (Peng et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent molecular work.

claim: S cones diverged evolutionarily from the common ancestor of LM cones far earlier than L and M cones diverged from each other.
source: Given that S cones diverged evolutionarily from the common ancestor of LM cones far earlier than L and M cones diverged from each other, it is not surprising that S cones differ more from LM cones than L and M cones differ from each other (Nathans et al., 1986).
evidence: This is supported by citation to evolutionary studies.

claim: Isomerization-like events in salamander L cones contribute significantly to their noise.
source: Specifically, isomerization-like events in salamander L cones contribute significantly to their noise
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Noise in primate LM cones is dominated by sources other than isomerization-like events.
source: while noise in primate LM cones is dominated by other sources (Schneeweis and Schnapf, 1999; Rieke and Baylor, 2000; Angueyra and Rieke, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Compared to L cones, salamander S cones have much lower noise, consistent with a more stable photopigment.
source: Compared to L cones, salamander S cones have much lower noise, consistent with a more stable photopigment.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The lower noise in salamander S cones is consistent with the expected wavelength dependence of photopigment stability.
source: This is consistent with the expected wavelength dependence of photopigment stability (Luo et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work on photopigment stability.

claim: Unlike the situation in salamander, the effective noise of primate S cones exceeds that of LM cones at low background-light levels.
source: Unlike the situation in salamander, the effective noise of primate S cones exceeds that of LM cones at low background-light levels (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a finding from noise measurements shown in Figure 7.

claim: Higher effective noise in primate S cones results in higher flash-detection thresholds for S vs LM cones.
source: This results in higher flash-detection thresholds for S vs LM cones.
evidence: This is an inference from the noise measurements.

claim: S- vs LM-cone photocurrents and voltages exhibited similar differences in kinetics, suggesting an origin largely from differences in the cone phototransduction machinery.
source: S- vs LM-cone photocurrents and voltages exhibited similar differences in kinetics (Figures 1–4), suggesting an origin largely from differences in the cone phototransduction machinery.
evidence: This is an inference from comparing current-clamp and voltage-clamp data.

claim: The kinetic differences in primate S vs LM cones are similar to salamander S vs L cones.
source: This is similar to salamander S vs L cones (Rieke and Baylor, 2000)
evidence: This is a comparison with prior work.

claim: The kinetic differences in primate S vs LM cones are different from goldfish S vs LM cones, in which kinetic differences originate from the expression of a hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide-gated (HCN) channel in LM but not S cones.
source: but different from goldfish S vs LM cones, in which kinetic differences originate from the expression of a hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide-gated (HCN) channel in LM but not S cones (Howlett et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a comparison with prior work.

claim: Mammalian rod photoreceptors evolved from S cones and the two photoreceptor types share several phototransduction components.
source: Mammalian rod photoreceptors evolved from S cones and the two photoreceptor types share several phototransduction components (Craft et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Primate rods and S cones share the same arrestin isoform (arrestin1) responsible for photopigment inactivation and hence recovery of the light response.
source: For instance, primate rods and S cones share the same arrestin isoform (arrestin1) responsible for photopigment inactivation and hence recovery of the light response.
evidence: This is established knowledge about photoreceptor biochemistry.

claim: S cones also express the cone arrestin isoform (arrestin3), but the expression is lower than that in LM cones.
source: S cones also express the cone arrestin isoform (arrestin3), but the expression is lower than that in LM cones (Craft et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Based on biochemical differences, S cones are thought to share functional features with both rods and LM cones.
source: Based on these and other biochemical differences, S cones are thought to share functional features with both rods and LM cones.
evidence: This is an inference from biochemical data.

claim: Both the rising and recovery phases differ between S- and LM-cone responses.
source: Both the rising and recovery phases differ between S- and LM-cone responses (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the normalized response analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The two phases of the light responses are primarily controlled by different aspects of the phototransduction cascade.
source: These two phases of the light responses are primarily controlled by different aspects of the phototransduction cascade.
evidence: This is established knowledge about phototransduction.

claim: The analysis of rising and recovery phases suggests that multiple components of the phototransduction cascade differ between S and LM cones.
source: Hence, this analysis suggests that multiple components of the phototransduction cascade differ between S and LM cones, much like the differences observed between mammalian rods and cones (Ingram et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference from the response analysis, supported by comparison with prior work.

claim: Responses of both rods and cones typically speed with increasing background-light level.
source: Responses of both rods and cones typically speed with increasing background-light level.
evidence: This is established knowledge about photoreceptor adaptation.

claim: The speeding of photoreceptor responses with background can largely be explained by the increase in the rate of cGMP turnover produced by background light.
source: This speeding can largely be explained by the increase in the rate of cGMP turnover produced by background light (Nikonov et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The constancy of the kinetics of the S-cone responses with increasing background suggests that either the cGMP-turnover rate contributes minimally to response kinetics, or one or more components of the phototransduction cascade must slow with background to compensate the expected increase in cGMP-turnover rate.
source: The constancy of the kinetics of the S-cone responses with increasing background (Figure 5) suggests that either the cGMP-turnover rate contributes minimally to response kinetics, or one or more components of the phototransduction cascade must slow with background to compensate the expected increase in cGMP-turnover rate.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism underlying the constant S-cone kinetics.

claim: Cones perform a complex transformation on their inputs.
source: Cones perform a complex transformation on their inputs (Endeman and Kamermans, 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The complex transformation performed by cones makes it difficult to differentiate their contributions from those of downstream circuitry to the computations that support vision.
source: thus making it difficult to differentiate their contributions from those of downstream circuitry to the computations that support vision (van Hateren, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: One approach to understanding retinal circuits is incorporating reliable predictions of cone responses into retinal models in an attempt to better define the inputs to downstream circuitry.
source: One approach to this issue is incorporating reliable predictions of cone responses into retinal models in an attempt to better define the inputs to downstream circuitry.
evidence: This is a methodological approach discussed in the context of modeling.

claim: Only recently has it become possible to use validated models of the differences in LM cones across the visual field.
source: Only recently has it become possible to use validated models of the differences in LM cones across the visual field (Sinha et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The results provide the information necessary to construct models that capture differences between different spectral types of primate cones.
source: Our results here expand upon this by providing the information necessary to construct models that capture differences between different spectral types of primate cones.
evidence: This is a statement about the implications of the current findings.

claim: Electrophysiological recordings were performed on primate retina obtained through the Tissue Distribution Program of the University of Washington's Regional Primate Research Center.
source: Electrophysiological recordings were performed on primate retina obtained through the Tissue Distribution Program of the University of Washington's Regional Primate Research Center.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about tissue sourcing.

claim: Recordings were made from retinas from Macaca fascicularis, Macaca nemestrina, and Macaca mulatta of both sexes, aged 2 through 20 years.
source: Recordings were made from retinas from Macaca fascicularis, Macaca nemestrina, and Macaca mulatta of both sexes, aged 2 through 20 years.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the animal subjects.

claim: S cones make up a minority of the cone photoreceptors within the primate retina.
source: S cones make up a minority of the cone photoreceptors within the primate retina.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge.

claim: S cones can be identified based on their morphology and position within the photoreceptor array, appearing slightly smaller, recessed, and out of place.
source: Although we did not use this approach to collect any of the data reported here, it did help us learn to identify S cones based on their morphology and position within the photoreceptor array (Ahnelt et al., 1987; Packer et al., 2010). Targeting cones that appeared slightly smaller, recessed, and out of place within the photoreceptor array dramatically increased the probability that the cones were S cones.
evidence: This is a methodological finding about S cone identification.

claim: The data reported here represents recordings from a total of 72 S cones, 60 M cones and 112 L cones from peripheral retina and 32 S cones, 25 M cones, and 28 L cones from foveal retina.
source: The data reported here represents recordings from a total of 72 S cones, 60 M cones and 112 L cones from peripheral retina and 32 S cones, 25 M cones, and 28 L cones from foveal retina.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about sample sizes.

claim: The minimum light level used (500 R*/cone/s) was sufficient to effectively eliminate rod responses.
source: The minimum light level used (500 R*/cone/s) was sufficient to effectively eliminate rod responses (Grimes et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a methodological detail supported by citation.
